A severe thunderstorm knocked down numerous trees and wires in Stroud Township. This was the start of a macroburst that affected eastern Monroe County. The wind damage started at the Pinebrook Bible Camp off of Pennsylvania State Route 191. About a dozen downed trees damaged a couple of buildings and vehicles. A second floor porch and stairway were damaged at one building. About 60 trees were uprooted within Stroud Township parks. A downed tree pulled down a wire that started a truck fire on Fremont Avenue and a downed tree fell across Roosevelt Street.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a large tree in East Stroudsburg on Pennsylvania State Route 447 near North Courtland Street and took down the mast arm of a traffic light.

The macroburst wind damage from the severe thunderstorm peaked in Smithfield Township. The worst damage was centered around Worthington Street and Minisink Road near River Road in the Shawnee on Delaware area of the township. Even century old locusts trees were knocked down. One home was seriously damaged by a downed tree as were three vehicles on the property. River Road was closed through the night between the entrance to the Shawnee Inn and Hollow Road due to downed trees and debris. Elsewhere in the township, another downed tree became embedded with a house on Redwood Lane and three trees fell across Roosevelt Street. The combination of lightning and damaging winds caused about 30,000 Pennsylvania Power and Light and Metropolitan Edison customers to lose power. Hardest outage hit townships were Jackson, Stroud, Stroudsburg and Tobyhanna.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a couple of trees in West Whiteland Township.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down several large trees in East Goshen Township.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down several trees in Nesquehoning Borough. Pennsylvania State Route 54 was closed in the Hauto area because of the downed trees.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down several trees in Lansford Borough also. One fell onto and damaged a vehicle.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down a couple of trees in Mahoning Township and forced the closure of Pennsylvania State Route 902, Mill Road, near Straus Valley Road.  There were still about 200 Pennsylvania Power and Light customers without power in Carbon County on the morning of the 8th.
Penny size hail fell in Summit Hill.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down trees and wires in Haddon Heights, Haddonfield and Audubon.
A severe thunderstorm dropped penny to quarter size hail in Whitehouse Station (Readington Township).
A lightning strike started a house fire in Ocean View (Dennis Township).

Lightning struck and injured a man standing on a porch during a thunderstorm on Townhouse Lane in Little Egg Harbor Township. He complained about chest and leg pain as well as overall weakness. Another lightning strike temporarily knocked off communications at the township police department after a roof antenna was struck.
For the third time in 2011, the water treatment plant in Allentown Borough was struck by lightning, This lightning strike fried computerized controls and caused about an estimated $40,000 in damages.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused brief flash flooding along the Franklin Creek. The Franklin Creek at Castor Avenue was above its 7 foot flood stage from 413 p.m. through 425 p.m. EDT on the 8th. It crested at 7.05 feet at 415 p.m. EDT. The heavy rain also caused flooding along Interstate 95 in the Bridesburg section of the city. Event precipitation totals included 1.85 inches in Center City and 1.48 inches at the Philadelphia International Airport. Doppler Radar storm total estimates of 2 to 3 inches occurred near the Franklin Creek basin.

Flash flooding forced the closure of the northbound lanes of Interstate 295 in Bellmawr.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused considerable urban and poor drainage flooding in western Camden County as well as flash flooding of smaller creeks. It wreaked havoc to the start of the weekend commute as it coincided with a Friday afternoon on the 8th. In Camden, Interstate 676 was closed in both directions. Flash flooding was also reported along Federal Street and the Admiral Wilson Boulevard. Flash flooding was also reported on the Admiral Wilson Boulevard in Pennsauken Township as well as State Route 38. In Gloucester City, U.S. Route 130 was closed at Interstate 76. In Bellmawr Borough, Southbound New Jersey State Route 42 (North-South Freeway) was closed due to flooding just south of Interstate 295. Eastbound 295 itself was closed due to flooding at Creek Road. ||In Pennsauken, a Skywarn spotter measure 1.75 inches of rain within 20 minutes. Event precipitation totals within Camden County included 3.82 inches in Berlin, 2.93 inches in Winslow and 1.97 inches in Merchantville.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused poor drainage and small stream flooding in central Gloucester County in and around Glassboro. A Skywarn spotter measured an event total of 4.00 inches in Glaassboro.  Other Gloucester County precipitation event totals included 3.07 inches in Mantua.

The runoff from heavier rain earlier in the day on the 8th caused minor flooding along the Cooper River in Haddonfield. The Cooper River in Haddonfield was above its 2.8 foot flood stage from 944 p.m. EDT on the 8th through 1216 a.m. EDT on the 9th. It crested at 2.84 feet at 1030 p.m. EDT on the 8th.   Event precipitation totals within Camden County included 3.82 inches in Berlin, 2.93 inches in Winslow and 1.97 inches in Merchantville.

A father and daughter suffered minor injuries after they were struck by lightning as they stood underneath a tree at the Moore Township Recreation Fields. The father was holding an umbrella over his daughter's head when they were both thrown to the ground by the lightning bolt. The father had burns on his feet, stomach and leg and felt numbness and a burning sensation. The daughter suffered a flash burn to her right eye.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down numerous trees in the Newport area of Downe Township.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down a couple of trees in Hopewell Township, one onto State Route 49 (Shiloh Pike).

A power surge from a lightning strike caused the Best Western Plus Allentown Inn to be closed until August 19th. The lightning strike caused the water heaters to malfunction which led to a small gas leak. Guests were relocated to other hotels and no injuries were reported.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a couple of trees and large tree limbs in Southampton Township.

A severe thunderstorm produced a strong wet microburst and knocked down numerous trees in Washington Township including one that fell onto a moving vehicle. The driver was not injured. The severe thunderstorm also caused the partial collapse of a couple of buildings.

A severe thunderstorm caused wind damage in Ocean City along Central and Ocean Avenues as well as along the beach. Part of the roof was torn away from the Seabreeze Apartments on Ocean Avenue. The roof of the Sun Aqua motel was also dislodged. The roof debris damaged a nearby condominium as well as the windshield of several vehicles. On Central Avenue, three homes suffered partial roof collapses and facade damage. The debris hit homes across the street. A utility pole collapsed. Wind damage also occurred to the 5th Street ballfield. On the beach itself, thirteen lifeguard stands were destroyed as they went tumbling down the beach. About a dozen beach patrol surf boats went cartwheeling down the beach also. Six were totally damaged. One was found in Strathmere. A wind gust of 66 mph was recorded within Ocean City. No serious injuries were reported.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down numerous trees in Monroe County from Coolbaugh Township southeast through Smithfield Township. Wind damage began in the Tobyhanna area of Coolbaugh Township as trees were knocked down. Numerous trees were knocked down in the Swiftwater area of Pocono Township. A downed tree blocked Echo Lake Road. Trees were knocked down across Pennsylvania State Route 314. In Stroud Township, trees were knocked down on Pennsylvania State Route 447 just north of Echo Lake Road. In Smithfield Township, multiple trees were knocked down on Brushy Mountain Road near Barren Road. Trees also blocked Kings Pond Road. The wind damage extended as far southeast at the Marshalls Creek area of Smithfield Township. About 3,200 electrical customers lost power, mainly in Paradise Valley (Paradise Township) and Analomink (Stroud Township).
Penny size hail fell in Tobyhanna.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused basement and stream flooding in and around Lehigh Township and Walnutport in northwestern Northampton County. Precipitation event totals included 6.00 inches in both Berlinsville and Walnutport.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding along the Monocacy Creek in Bethlehem. The thunderstorms also caused poor drainage flooding in Northampton County.  The Monocacy Creek in Bethlehem was above its 4.5 foot flood from 456 p.m. EDT through 725 p.m. EDT on the 25th. It crested at 5.19 feet at 6 p.m. EDT. Event precipitation totals included 3.74 inches in Forks Township, 3.70 inches in Bethlehem, 3.48 inches in Easton and 2.53 inches in Martins Creek.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused poor drainage flooding and creek flooding within Philadelphia. The Frankford Creek at Castor Avenue was briefly above its 7 foot flood stage from 829 p.m. through 832 p.m. EDT on the 25th. It crested at 7.06 at 830 p.m. EDT. The Pennypack Creek at the Rhawn Street Bridge was above its 7 foot flood stage from 104 a.m. EDT through 158 a.m. EDT on the 26th. It crested at 7.11 feet at 130 a.m. EDT. Event precipitation totals included 1.37 inches in Northeast Philadelphia.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused poor drainage flooding as well as flooding of creeks in eastern Chester County. West Chester was one of the hardest hit municipalities with several water rescues as vehicles became stranded in flood waters. Flooding was reported on Adams, Franklin, Miner, Bolmar, Washington and Market Streets as well as Bradford and Hannum (U.S. Route 322) Avenues and the West Chester By Pass (U.S. Route 202). Farther to the northeast, the Valley Creek at Valley Forge was above its 7 foot flood stage from 938 p.m. EDT through 1032 p.m. EDT on the 25th. It crested at 7.2 feet at 10 p.m. EDT.  Event precipitation totals included 4.26 inches in Exton and 2.03 inches in West Chester.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down several large trees in Lansdale. A downed tree damaged a home and vehicle on one property.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down multiple trees along South Valley Forge Road in Towamencin Township. One large tree fell onto a house.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down several trees in the Woodlands Community around Welsh and Village Roads as well as on Ash Lane in Horsham Township. A couple of trees were also knocked down in Upper Gwynned Township.

A powerful and damaging microburst occurred in Vernon Township during the early evening of the 29th. Estimated maximum wind speeds were 90 mph. Wind damage began near Silver Fox Lane and moved southeast for about two miles and ended near the intersection of State Route 94 and Sand Hill Road. Most of the wind damage was downed trees, estimated at over one thousand as well as downed wires. Several homes sustained roof damage from the combination of either trees falling on them, or the winds themselves. In the Tall Timbers Mobile Home Park, a number of trees also fell on vehicles and damaged mobile homes. One home on Edsall Drive suffered significant roof damage. The family was taken in by the Crystal Springs Resort. A few other families in the area had to leave their home because of wind damage.  An amateur radio antenna on Edsall Drive was bent in half.  In addition to Edsall Drive, tree wind damage was extensive on Black Walnut Mountain Road, Basswood Drive and Shebe Drive. About 2,000 Jersey Central Power and Light Customers lost power, 500 still did not have power restored on the afternoon of the 30th.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a couple of trees and wires in the Burlhome section of Philadelphia. One downed wire started a vehicle fire.
Quarter size hail fell from a severe thunderstorm in Brick Township.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down about a half a dozen trees in Trenton. One downed tree at the Trenton Transit Center on Walnut Street trapped a cab driver within his vehicle. He was not injured.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down trees and tree limbs in Moorestown. A couple of roadways near the Delran Township border were closed  due to tree debris.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a few trees and tree limbs in Mount Laurel Township. One downed tree on Rancocas Boulevard fell through the roof of a house.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down numerous trees, tree limbs and wires in Willingboro Township. There were about 50 thunderstorm related calls throughout the township. One downed tree on Twig Court fell through a home and damaged a vehicle. Westbound Garfield Road remained closed through the 30th.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a few trees in Jackson Township and damaged a couple of homes and vehicles.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down hundreds of trees and tree limbs in Brick Township and cause property damage to dozens of properties. The Forge Pond, Birchwood Park and Mantaloking neighborhoods were hardest hit. Downed trees (some damaging homes) were reported on Leeswing Drive, Chambers Bridge Road, Sprucewood Drive and Ashwood Drive. The hospital in Brick had to run on emergency generator power for hours after power was lost. A cooling center was also opened in the township.

A severe thunderstorm caused tree and roof damage in Lakewood Township. Around sixty people were evacauated from the Peter Ward Tower on Woehr Street after a large part of the apartment building's roof was blown away. A shelter was opened at the Lakewood High School. The residents were permitted to return on August 1st. The Atlantic Coast Rehabilitation Center Nursing Home was evacuated after they lost power.
A lightning strike split a tree into pieces on Cypress Lane in Hamilton Township. The downed tree blocked the back door and porch of the home.
A lightning strike started a fire at an occupied structure at the intersection of Ford Road and U.S. Route 9 in Howell Township.
A lightning strike started an attic fire at a house on Melissa Court in Moorestown. The fire was contained in the attic and no injuries were reported.
A pair of lightning strikes caused house fires on Emerald Lane and Helm Turn in Willingboro Township. The latter home was rendered uninhabitable by the fire and the family dog also perished in it.

A 32-year-old man was struck and seriously injured by lightning while on a beach in Sandy Hook. He had come ashore from an ocean swim when he was struck. He was revived by emergency personnel that used a defibrillator and then sent to the Monmouth Medical Center.

An EF-0 tornado touched down in Millstone Township in Monmouth County. The tornado initially touched down north of Buono Farm and tracked northeast where it crossed New Jersey State Route 33.and damaged a flag pole and a business fencing.  A barn was damaged on Prodelin Way. Numerous trees and some wires were knocked down along its path, especially on Prodelin and Arrowhead Ways and Bergen Mills Road. The tornado moved along Arrowhead Way before it lifted. The tornado's approximate path length was 1.7 miles, maximum path width of 50 yards and estimated maximum wind speed of 70 mph. No deaths or injuries were reported.

Lightning struck and went through the wiring of the home, found a weak spot in a crawl space underneath the first floor and started the fire.  A water pipe also burst inside the house. No injuries were reported, but the two residents of the house were provided shelter for the evening. The residents next door were also evacuated  due to the heavy smoke.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down numerous trees and tree limbs in eastern Lehigh County from Coplay Borough and Whitehall and South Whitehall Townships southward into Allentown. A concentration of downed trees was reported near the Whitehall High School. Four homes were damaged by downed trees in Whitehall Township and one in Coplay Borough. Trees were knocked down along Cedar Crest Boulevard in South Whitehall Township. In North Catasauqua, numerous large limbs were knocked down within the borough park. Tree damage occurred on the property of Saint Andrew's Roman Catholic Church and a roadway sign was flipped along Grove Street.  About 2,900 Pennsylvania Power and Light customers lost power in the county.

A Skywarn spotter measured a wind gust of 52 mph at his house in Cream Ridge. The combination of lightning and damaging winds caused about 400 homes throughout Monmouth to lose power.

A series of thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused flash flooding of smaller streams and fields in the Cohansey Creek basin in western Cumberland County. The heaviest rain fell in Greenwich, Hopewell and Stow Creek Townships. Actual storm totals included 3.14 inches in Greenwich Township and 2.29 inches in Bridgeton.

Two 25-year-old men drowned in Hockessin after attempting to run home through the storm across a branch of the Mill Creek on the night of the 27th. Their bodies were recovered near Wilmington on the afternoon of the 29th. Delaware State Route 9 was badly flooded in the county.||The White Clay Creek at Newark was above its 11.5 foot flood stage from 208 a.m. EDT through Noon EDT on the 28th. It crested at 14.64 feet at 530 a.m. EDT. It was the highest crest since the remnants of Hurricane Jeanne in late September of 2004. Farther downstream, the White Clay Creek downstream of Newark had record breaking major flooding with a crest of 17.20 feet at 815 a.m. EDT on the 28th.  The previous record was set during Hurricane Floyd in September of 1999.  The creek was above its 13 foot flood stage from 1044 p.m. EDT on the 27th through 423 p.m. EDT on the 28th. ||The Red Clay Creek had major flooding, its worst flooding since the remnants of Hurricane Jeanne in late September of 2004 and the fourth highest crest on record. The Red Clay Creek at Wooddale was above its 7 foot flood stage from 1106 p.m. EDT on the 27th through 1240 p.m. EDT on the 28th. It crested at 12.99 feet at 645 a.m. EDT on the 28th. Farther downstream, the Red Clay Creek at Stanton was above its 15 foot flood stage from 1039 p.m. EDT on the 27th through 346 p.m. EDT on the 28th.  It crested at 23.18 feet at 745 a.m. EDT on the 28th.||The Christina River at Coochs Bridge had record breaking major flooding with a crest of 13.89 feet at 415 a.m. EDT on the 28th.  The previous record was set with Hurricane Floyd in September of 1999. The river was above its 10.5 foot flood stage from 909 p.m. EDT on the 27th through 1143 a.m. EDT on the 28th. The Brandywine Creek at Wilmington had moderate  flooding and a record breaking crest of18.71 feet at 230 p.m. EDT on the 28th. The creek  was above its 16.5 foot flood stage from 454 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 417 a.m. EDT on the 29th.||Event rainfall totals included 8.12 inches in Clayton, 7.85 inches in Armstrong, 7.80 inches in Middletown, 7.00 inches in Newport and 6.94 inches at the New Castle County Airport.

Flooding drowned several thousand chickens in Felton. Delaware State Route 6 was flooded in Smyrna and Delaware State Route 9 was flooded in Little Creek. Mirror Lake also flooded in Dover. Event rainfall totals included 10.08 inches in Marydel, 8.55 inches in Smyrna, 6.93 inches in Dover, 5.26 inches in Magnolia and 4.90 inches in Felton.

The Nanticoke River at Bridgeville was above its 8 foot flood stage from 905 a.m. on the 28th through 207 p.m. EDT on the 29th. It crested at 8.73 feet at 8 p.m. EDT on the 28th. The Beaver Dam Ditch at Camly Road was above its 9 foot flood stage from 1203 p.m. EDT on the 28th through 1107 a.m. EDT on the 30th. It crested at 11.74 feet at 820 a.m. EDT on the 29th.                                      ||Event rainfall totals included 9.83 inches in Greenwood, 8.72 inches in Delmar, 7.78 inches in Cokesbury, 7.40 inches in Seaford, 6.00 inches in Lewes, and 5.60 inches at the Georgetown Airport.

An EF1 tornado touched down in the Quakertown area near Lewes during the early evening of the 27th. This tornado was embedded within convective bands associated with Hurricane Irene. About 50 homes were damaged and several vehicles and sheds were either damaged or destroyed. The tornado touched down near the eastern end of Tradewinds Lane, then moved west along Tradewinds Lane, crossed Delaware State Route 269A before lifting at Crab Apple Lane. Numerous trees were uprooted or snapped along this path, and numerous homes experienced shingle damage in the Tradewinds, Donovan Smith, Swanendael Acres and Nassau Station Developments. The most significant damage occurred on Crab Apple Lane where a house sustained substantial roof damage with its rafters exposed. The house's garage was also ripped away.||The tornado path length was estimated at 0.7 miles, its maximum path width was 80 yards and its estimated maximum wind speed was 95 mph. No serious injuries were reported.

The Big Elk Creek flooded businesses in Elkton on and around South Bridge Street. The Big Elk Creek at Elk Mills had moderate flooding and was above its 9 foot flood stage from 1157 p.m. EDT on the 27th through 931 a.m. EDT on the 28th. It crested at 10.31 feet at 1245 a.m. EDT on the 28th. Event rainfall totals included 7.19 inches in Cherry Hill, 6.86 inches in Fair Hills and 5.74 inches in Elkton.

About a dozen roadways were closed by flooding. In Millington (along the Chester River) the flooding was described as the worst since Hurricane Floyd. Several people were rescued from stranded vehicles. The Sassafras River also flooded along the county line with Cecil County.
Flooding rains forced the closure of Maryland State Route 300 at Dudley Corner Road.  Event rainfall totals included 4.70 inches in Stevensville.

Flooding rains forced the closure of sections of Maryland State Routes 565A, 329, 328 and 33. The combination of flooding and tropical storm winds damaged 100 properties and 50 roadways and bridges   Roadway damage alone was estimated at $750,000. The Raritan River at Manville was above its 14 foot flood stage from 443 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 905 p.m. EDT on the 29th. It crested at 26.29 feet at 400 p.m. EDT on the 28th.  Farther downstream, the Raritan River at Bound Brook was above its 28 foot flood stage from 310 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 336 a.m. EDT on the 30th. It crested at 41.90 feet at 6 p.m. EDT on the 28th.  ||The Millstone River had major flooding and its highest crest on record at Griggstown and Blackwells Mills.  The Millstone River at Griggstown  was above its 10 foot flood stage from 1154 p.m. EDT on the 27th through 740 a.m. EDT on the 31st. It crested at 24.21 feet at 200 p.m. EDT on the 28th. Farther downstream, the Millstone River at Blackwells Mills was above its 9 foot flood stage from 338 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 803 p.m. EDT on the 30th. It crested at 21.24 feet at 630 p.m. EDT on the 28th.  Farther downstream, the Millstone River at Weston was above its 12.4 foot flood stage from 504 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 225 a.m. EDT on the 30th. It crested at 22.91 feet at 715 p.m. EDT on the 28th.   | |The Pike Run at Belle Mead was above its 7 flood stage from 1112 p.m. EDT on the 27th through 120 a.m. EDT on the 28th.  It crested at 9.73 feet at 1230 a.m. EDT pm the 28th. The Pike Run at Belle Mead was again above its 7 foot flood stage from 1122 a.m. EDT through 1247 p.m. EDT on the 28th. It crested at 8.13 feet at 1130 a.m. EDT.  The Green Brook at Seeley Mills had its third  highest crest on record. The brook was above its 5.5 foot flood stage multiple times between 144 a.m. EDT and 945 a.m. EDT on the 28th. It crested at 6.46 feet at 845 a.m. EDT.  The Stony Brook at Watchung had its fourth  highest crest on record. The brook was above its 14.5 foot flood between 1230 a.m. EDT and 848 a.m. EDT on the 28th. It crested at 16.38 feet at145 a.m. EDT.||Event rainfall totals included 8.19 inches in Bedminster Township, 7.65 inches in Hillsborough Township, 7.56 inches in Somerville, 7.56 inches in Franklin Township and 7.55 inches in Bridgewater Township.

Both the Musconetcong and Paulinskill Rivers flooded. The Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area was closed through Labor Day Weekend (September 5th). The Delaware River at Tocks Island had moderate flooding and was above its 21 foot flood stage from 1018  p.m. EDT on the 28th through 742 p.m. EDT on the 29th. It crested at 23.21 feet at 1245 p.m. EDT on the 29th.  Farther downstream, the Delaware River at Phillipsburg had minor flooding and was above its 22 foot flood stage from 843 p.m. EDT on the 28th through 1210 a.m. EDT on the 30th. It crested at 25.15 feet at 5 a.m. EDT on the 29th. Farther downstream, the Delaware River at Reigelsville also had minor flooding and was above its 22 foot flood stage from 922 p.m. EDT on the 28th through 219 a.m. EDT on the 30th. It crested at 24.56 feet at 630  a.m. EDT on the 29th.||Event rainfall totals included 7.15 inches in Mansfield Township, 6.82 inches in White Township, 6.65 inches in Greenwich Township, 6.56 inches in Blairstown Township and 6.56 inches in Franklin Township.

Flooding affected Branchville, Frankford, Hampton, Hardyston, Newton, Ogdensburg and Vernon the hardest in Sussex County.  Flooding forced the closure of numerous roadways in the county including U.S. Route 206 as well as state and county routes 94, 15, 23, 517 and 628. Branchville was literally cut off after flooding occurred along the Dry Brook. About 100 people were evacuated within the Borough. Half a dozen bridges were either damaged or totally washed out. In Vernon Township, eight families were cut off after another bridge washed out. Four bridges were also washed out in Frankford Township.   ||The Flat Brook at Flatbrookville had major flooding and its second highest crest since Hurricane Diane in 1955. The brook was above its 6 foot flood stage from 810 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 404 p.m. EDT on the 29th. It crested at 10.59 feet at 1215 a.m. EDT on the 29th.||Event rainfall totals included 7.93 inches in Wantage Township, 7.87 inches in Hardyston Township, 7.33 inches in Woodbourne, 7.17 inches in Andover Township, 6.69 inches in Vernon Twp and 6.53 inches in Montague Township.

Morris County was greatly effected by flooding from Irene, especially along the Passaic and Pompton Rivers. |In Dover Township, a construction worker fell off a bridge, was washed away and drowned in the Rockaway River. About 4,000 homes in the county were affected by flood waters in Pequannock, Lincoln Park, Dover, Parsippany and Denville. The flooding along the Rockaway River forced the collapse of the northbound Interstate 287 roadway shoulder in Boonton. All northbound lanes remained closed until August 30th. In Hanover Township, a 177-yearold historic First Presbyterian Church of Whippany suffered approximately about $350,000 in damages, one of the hardest hit structures in the county.||Full scale evacuations occurred in Pequannock Township and Lincoln Park Borough. In Pequannock, over 800 homes were damaged by flood waters, many had four to six feet of water on their first floor. In Denville, 500 homes were flooded and damaged. Other homes were damaged in Dover and Pine Brook. In Parsippany, the National Guard was needed to rescue people from two flooded hotels. Other major roadways that were closed due to flooding included New Jersey State Routes 10, 23, 46 and 53. ||The Pompton River had major flooding and record breaking crests throughout its entire length, surpassing the flooding that occurred during April of 1984.  The Pompton River at Pompton Plains crested at a record breaking 25.24 feet at 115 a.m. EDT on the 29th. It was above its 16 foot flood stage from 115 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 245 a.m. EDT on the 31st.  Farther downstream, the Pompton River at Ryerson Road crested at a record breaking 20.47 feet at 1140 p.m. EDT on the 28th. It was above its 12 foot flood stage from 713 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 602 a.m. EDT on September 3rd.   Farther downstream, the Pompton River at Midwood crested at a record breaking 17.31 feet at 630 p.m. EDT on the 29th. It was above its 7.5 foot flood stage from 634 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 845 p.m. EDT on September 5th. Farther downstream, the Pompton River at the Mountainview Bridge crested at a record breaking 16.08 feet at 420 p.m. EDT on the 29th. It was above its 8 foot flood stage from 908 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 739 a.m. EDT on September 4th. |||The Rockaway River above the Boonton Reservoir had major flooding and a record breaking crest of 9.31 feet at 7 p.m. EDT on the 28th. The previous record was set in April of 1984. The river was above its 5 foot flood stage from 531 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 1137 a.m. EDT on the 30th.  The Rockaway River below the Boonton Reservoir also had major flooding and also a record breaking crest of 9.73 feet at 1045 p.m. EDT on the 28th. The previous record was set in January of 1979. The river was above its 5 foot flood stage from 628 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 816 p.m. EDT on the 31st.|||The Passaic River at Millington and Pine Brook had major flooding and record breaking crests. The Passaic River at Chatham had moderate flooding. The Passaic River at Millington record breaking crest of 10.26 feet occurred at 1 p.m. EDT on the 29th. It was above its 8 foot flood stage from 708 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 407 a.m. EDT on September 1st.  The Passaic River at Chatham  was above its 6 foot flood stage from 232 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 930 a.m. EDT on September 3rd.  It crested at 7.76 feet at 1245 p.m. EDT on the 29th.  The Passaic River at Pine Brook record breaking crest of 24.12 feet occurred at 730 a.m. EDT on the 30th. It was above its 19 foot flood stage from 730 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 1115 p.m. EDT on September 5th, just before the rains from Tropical Storm Lee arrived. The Passaic River was the last river and Pine Brook was the last location on the river to go below flood stage. Just downstream of Morris County along the Passaic and Union County line, the Passaic River at Two Bridges also had major flooding and a record breaking crest of 17.17 feet at 515 a.m. EDT on the 30th. It was above its 9 foot flood stage from 7 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 815 a.m. EDT on September 5th.    ||The Whippany Creek at Morristown had major flooding and a record breaking crest of 9.58 feet at 930 a.m. EDT on the 28th. The creek  was above its 6 foot flood stage from 105 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 1233 a.m. EDT on the 29th.  The Pequannock River at the Macopin Dam had moderate flooding and was above its 5.5 foot flood stage from 259 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 237 p.m. EDT on the 30th. It crested at 7.42 feet at 245 p.m. EDT on the 28th.  The East Ditch at Beaver Brook Road had major flooding and set an all-time record high crest. It was above its 2.5 foot flood stage from 902 p.m. EDT on the 27th through 521 a.m. EDT on the 31st. It crested at 5.50 feet at 850 a.m. EDT on the 28th.||Event rainfall totals included 10.52 inches in Jefferson Township, 9.33 inches in Chatham, 9.30 inches in Morris Township, 9.02 inches in Randolph Township and 8.94 inches in Roxbury Township.

An EF-0 tornado touched down in Robbinsville Township about 3 a.m. EDT on the 28th.  The tornado touched down in a Mercer County Park, crossed Perrineville Road and lifted just southwest of Woods Road. Numerous trees were knocked down, along with several electric poles and  wires. Damage was concentrated on the 500 block of Perrineville Road.  The estimated path length was six tenths of a mile, the maximum path width was thirty yards and the estimated maximum wind speed was 85 mph.
