events.event_narrative: Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding along the Lizard Creek in East Penn Township. Pennsylvania State Route 895 was flooded by the creek and closed. Event precipitation totals included 4.45 inches in Lower Towamensing Township, 3.98 inches in Bowmanstown and 3.92 inches in Palmerton.

The runoff from the heavier rain earlier in the afternoon caused flooding in northeast Morris County. The East Ditch at Beaver Brook Road was above its 2.5 foot flood stage from 440 p.m. EDT through 850 p.m. EDT on the 9th. It crested at 2.70 feet at 525 p.m. EDT. Event precipitation totals included 2.29 inches in Long Hill Township, 1.98 inches in Denville and 1.76 inches in Rockaway.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding and road closures in eastern Somerset County. Road closures were reported in Bound Brook, Bridgewater, Manville and Montgomery. Several vehicular rescues were performed. All roads were reopened by 5 p.m. EDT. Event precipitation totals included 2.33 inches in Franklin Township, 2.07 inches in Hillsborough Township and 2.02 inches in Bridgewater Township and Somerville.

Flash flooding along the Monocacy Creek caused the evacuation of vendors at the Musikfest in the historical district in Bethlehem. Both the Handwerkplatz and Volksplatz were evacuated and canceled for the 14th. Some vendors lost jewelry, tubs and tablecloths. Vehicles were flooded as was some electrical equipment and tents. Several booths and propane tanks were swept away. No injuries were reported. The Monocacy Creek at Bethlehem was above its 4.5 foot flood stage from 1140 p.m. EDT on the 13th through 335 a.m. EDT on the 14th. It crested at 5.18 feet at 1 a.m. EDT on the 14th. Precipitation event totals included 5.20 inches in Bethlehem, 5.18 inches in Nazareth and 4.53 inches in Glendon.

Runoff from the heavier rain overnight and more showers and thunderstorms during the morning of the 14th caused renewed flooding along the Monocacy Creek. The Monocacy Creek at Bethlehem was above its 4.5 foot flood stage again from 852 a.m. EDT through 1102 a.m. EDT on the 14th. It crested at 4.57 feet at 945 a.m. EDT. Two day precipitation event totals included 5.20 inches in Bethlehem, 5.18 inches in Nazareth and 4.53 inches in Glendon.

Thunderstorms with very heavy rain caused roadway flooding and flash flooding of smaller streams in Albany, Greenwich, Tilden and Windsor Townships as well as Hamburg across the northern tier of Berks County. A few homes were also flooded and a mud slide was reported in Hamburg. Event precipitation totals included 4.17 inches in Hamburg.

Thunderstorms with very heavy rain caused roadway flooding and flash flooding of smaller streams across the central third of Lehigh County from Allentown, Bethlehem and Hanover westnorthwest through all of the Whitehall Townships as well as Lowhill and Weisenberg Townships. In Allentown, the heavy rain caused a roof collapse and the evacuation of thirteen people. Event precipitation totals included 4.24 inches at the Lehigh Valley International Airport, 3.90 inches in Allentown and 3.73 inches in Schnecksville.

The runoff from heavy rain earlier in the day caused flooding along the Darby Creek and closed MacDade Boulevard in Darby. Flooding was also reported in Clifton Heights between Baltimore Avenue and Springfield Road. Event precipitation totals included 6.13 in Nether Providence Township and 2.86 inches in Aston.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms caused flash flooding along the Pennypack and in particular Frankford Creek in Philadelphia. The Frankford Creek at Castor Avenue was above its 7 foot flood stage from 705 a.m. EDT through 737 a.m. EDT on the 14th. It crested at 8.08 feet at 715 a.m. EDT. The Pennypack Creek at the Rhawn Street Bridge was above its 7 foot flood stage from 651 a.m. EDT through 821 p.m. EDT on the 14th. It crested at 7.64 feet at 415 p.m. EDT. Event precipitation totals included 5.80 inches in Rockledge and at the Philadelphia International Airport and 4.18 inches in Wyndmoor.

Runoff flooding from heavy rain continued on the Pennypack Creek through the afternoon and into the evening of the 14th. The Pennypack Creek at the Rhawn Street Bridge was above its 7 foot flood stage from 651 a.m. EDT through 821 p.m. EDT on the 14th. It crested at 7.64 feet at 415 p.m. EDT. Event precipitation totals included 5.80 inches in Rockledge and at the Philadelphia International Airport and 4.18 inches in Wyndmoor.
Quarter size hail fell in Galloway Township.
A severe thunderstorm tore down large trees and wires in West Chester.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down large tree limbs and wires in Georgetown.

Repeated thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding in the central and northern parts of Queen Anne's County. Sixteen roadways were closed throughout the county because of flooding and included parts of Maryland State Routes 19, 213, 290 and 544. Spaniard Neck Road washed away near Centreville. Other county roads that were closed included Coleman Road, Hoffecker Road, Pine Tree Road, Pondtown Road, Flat Iron Square Road, Lands End Road, Round Top Road, Clabber and Pinder Hill Roads. Four  roadways remained closed on Monday the 15th. Vehicles were stuck in high water and some rescues were performed, but no serious injuries were reported. Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached around seven inches in the northwest part of Queen Anne's County around Kingstown.

Repeated thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding of roadways, streams and fields in the central and eastern parts of Kent County.  Roadway flooding and closures were reported around the intersection of Maryland State Routes 290 and 291 south of Chesterville. Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached around seven inches in the northern part of Kent County between Betterton and Georgetown.

Repeat thunderstorms with heavy rain dropped around six inches of rain across most of the southern third of New Castle County and three to six inches across the remainder of the county. This caused small stream, field and poor drainage flash flooding. A vehicle became stuck in flood waters in Christiana. Sections of Governor Printz Boulevard near Wilmington and Delaware State Route 7 were flooded. Event precipitation totals included 7.67 inches in Middletown, 7.38 inches in Blackbird, 6.32 inches in Glasgow, 5.47 inches in Newark and 3.13 inches at the New Castle County Airport.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding of smaller streams and roadways in southern Warren County, mainly in Lopatcong, Greenwich and Pohatcong Townships, Alpha Borough and Phillipsburg. Event precipitation totals included 5.30 inches in Washington Township, 4.74 inches in Greenwich Township and 4.08 inches in Phillipsburg.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding of smaller streams and roadways in northwestern Hunterdon County, mainly in Alexandria, Bethlehem, Holland and Union Townships. Event precipitation totals included 5.23 inches in Bethlehem Township, 5.18 inches in Califon, 4.59 inches in High Bridge and 4.36 inches in Clinton.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding of smaller streams and roadways in southern Somerset County. The runoff from the heavy rain caused flooding along the Millstone River later that day. The Pike Run at Belle Mead was above its 7 flood stage from 653 a.m. EDT through 1046 a.m. EDT on the 14th. It crested at 7.25 feet at 930 a.m. EDT.  Event precipitation totals included 5.86 inches in Montgomery Township, 4.61 inches in Hillsborough Township and 4.13 inches in Franklin Township.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of roadways and streams in northeastern Morris County during the morning of the 14th. The runoff flooding continued into the morning of the 16th. The East Ditch at Beaver Brook Road was above its 2.5 foot flood stage from 1005 a.m. EDT on the 14th through 817 a.m. EDT on the 16th. It crested at 3.13 feet at 1050  p.m. EDT on the 14th. Event precipitation totals included 4.45 inches in Long Hill Township, 4.08 inches in Denville, 3.79 inches in Morris Township, 3.75 inches in Chatham and 3.47 inches in Parsippany.

Runoff from a series of thunderstorms from overnight on the 13th through the morning of the 16th caused poor drainage and creek flooding in northeast Morris County. The East Ditch at Beaver Brook Road was above its 2.5 foot flood stage from 1005 a.m. EDT on the 14th  through 817 a.m. EDT on the 16th. It crested at 3.13 feet at 1050  p.m. EDT on the 14th. Seventy-two hour precipitation event totals through the morning of the 16th included 6.09 inches in Denville, 5.29 inches in Long Hill Township, 5.15 inches in Mine Hill Township, 5.01 inches in Parsippany, 4.75 inches in Morris Township, 4.54 inches in Chatham and 3.98 inches in Boonton.

Runoff from a series of thunderstorms from overnight on the 13th through the morning of the 16th caused poor drainage and river flooding, first along Pike Run in Belle Mead and then moderate flooding along the Millstone River. ||The Millstone River at Griggstown and Blackwells Mills had moderate flooding. The Millstone River at Griggstown was above its 10 foot flood stage from 145 p.m. EDT on the 14th through 1230 a.m. EDT on the 17th. It crested at 13.99 feet at 415 a.m. EDT on the 15th. Farther downstream, the Millstone River at Blackwells Mills was above its 9 foot flood stage from 105 a.m. EDT on the 15th through 620 a.m. EDT on the 16th. It crested at 10.26 feet at 845 a.m. EDT on the 15th.  The Pike Run at Belle Mead was above its 7 flood stage from 653 a.m. EDT through 1046 a.m. EDT on the 14th. It crested at 7.25 feet at 930 a.m. EDT.|Seventy-two hour event precipitation totals ending the morning of the 16th included 6.68 inches in Montgomery Township, 6.58 inches in Hillsborough Township 4.92 inches in Franklin Township and 4.75 inches in Bridgewater Township.   .

Runoff from heavy rain that fell mainly during the first half of the day and early afternoon on the 14th led to flooding along the Assunpink Creek that evening. The Assunpink Creek in Trenton was above its 8.5 foot flood stage from 600 p.m. EDT through 1151 p.m. EDT on the 14th  It crested at 8.82 feet at 930 p.m. EDT. Event precipitation totals included.

Thunderstorms with repeated torrential downpours caused flash flooding with damaging effects across eastern Salem County, especially in Pittsgrove Township. A county state of emergency was declared. At least one water rescue was reported. Flooding was reported in Alloway, Pittsgrove, Elmer and Upper Pittsgrove Townships. Fourteen roadways, nine bridges and many culverts were damaged, most in Pittsgrove Township. Some families were evacuated in Pittsgrove Township around Palatine and Centerton Lakes. Two bridges washed away in the township on Greenville and Burlington Roads. It was expected to take six to twelve months for both bridges to be replaced. Two other township roadways remained closed into the 19th. In spite of being drained prior to the rain, Centeron Lake filled and flooded. A few homes were half submerged by flood waters along Palatine Lake. In Elmer, Elmer Lake also flooded. Event precipitation totals included 9.64 inches in Elmer and 5.89 inches in Woodstown.

Repeat thunderstorms with heavy rain dropped around six inches of rain across most of the northern third of Kent County. This caused small stream, field and poor drainage flash flooding. Several roads were flooded and closed from near Dover northward. Delaware State Route 6 was closed near Clayton as was Main Street within Clayton itself. Just south of Smyrna, the northbound exit off of Delaware State Route 1 was closed. Event precipitation totals included 5.11 inches in Smyrna and 3.98 inches in Kenton.

Thunderstorms with repeated torrential downpours caused flash flooding of roadways, streams and basements in the southern half of Gloucester County. Roadway flooding was reported in Pitman, Glassboro, Franklin, Washington and Monroe Townships. In Malaga (Franklin Township),  U.S. Route 40 and New Jersey State Route 47 were flooded. The latter was still closed on the 15th. Conrail train service was stopped because of a sinkhole. In Glassboro, the foundation of a house on Deptford Drive collapsed. A motorist was rescued from flood waters on Delsea Drive (New Jersey State Route 47) near Clayton. In Clayton itself, a house became unstable because of its undermined foundation on North Main Street. In Williamstown (Monroe Township), flooding was reported along the Black Horse Pike (New Jersey State Route 42). Flooding also commenced along the Raccoon Creek. Event precipitation totals included 8.53 inches in Franklin Township and 5.92 inches in Woolwich Township.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused street and small stream flash flooding along the northern tier of Atlantic County and affected Hammonton Township the hardest. Four roadways: Fairview Avenue, Orchard Street, Second Street and Railroad Avenue were closed. heavy rain also affected Folsom, Buena and Buena Vista Township. Event precipitation totals included 7.51 inches in Hammonton and 2.15 inches in Buena Vista Township.

The runoff from the heavy rain caused the greatest flooding along the Raccoon Creek since August 10, 1967. The Raccoon Creek at Swedesboro had its second highest crest on record since that date. The creek was above its 13 foot flood stage from 127 p.m. EDT on the 14th  through 907 a.m. EDT on the 15th. It crested at 15.96 feet at 715 p.m. EDT on the 14th.

Runoff flooding from the torrential downpours persisted through the day on the 14th. Flooding then also started along the Maurice River. The Maurice River at Norma had major flooding and the second highest crest on record. The river at Norma was above its 4 foot flood stage from 105 a.m. EDT on the 15th through 145 a.m. EDT on the 19th. It crested at 6.33 feet at 125 p.m. EDT on the 16th.

Runoff flooding from the torrential downpours persisted through the day on the 14th in western Cumberland County. Flooding then also started along the Maurice River. The Maurice River at Norma had major flooding and the second highest crest on record. The river at Norma was above its 4 foot flood stage from 105 a.m. EDT on the 15th through 145 a.m. EDT on the 19th. It crested at 6.33 feet at 125 p.m. EDT on the 16th.

Runoff from the torrential downpours, especially in the headwaters of the Great Egg Harbor River, led to record breaking and major flooding at the Folsom gage site on the 16th. The Great Egg Harbor River at Folsom was above its 6 foot flood stage from 231 p.m. EDT on the 15th through 415 p.m. EDT on the 17th. It crested at 8.18 feet at 530 a.m. EDT on the 16th.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused poor drainage and small creek flooding in central and eastern Monmouth Counties in Long Branch, Neptune, Ocean and Middletown Townships. Several major roads were flooded and closed and water rescues were performed. In Long Branch, five vehicles became stuck in flood waters.  In Neptune Township, both New Jersey State Routes 33 and 35 flooded. In Ocean Township, three roadways flooded and in Middletown Township, southbound New Jersey State Route 35 was closed as was Palmer Avenue between New Jersey State Routes 35 and 36.  Event precipitation totals included 5.55 inches in Ocean Township,  5.51 inches in Red Bank, 4.78 inches in Rumson, 4.66 inches in Long Branch, 4.29 inches in Middletown Township and 3.82 inches in Belmar.

Runoff from the heavy rain on the 14th caused flooding along the Manasquan River into the 15th. The Manasquan River at Squankum was above its 7.5 foot flood stage from 1018 p.m. EDT on the 14th  through 435 a.m. EDT on the 15th. It crested at 7.67 feet at 1215 a.m. EDT on the 15th.

Thunderstorms with repeated torrential downpours caused flash flooding of roadways and streams in the western part of Cumberland County and affected Upper Deerfield Township and Bridgeton the hardest where two dams failed. This led to the evacuation of residents along the Cohansey River in Bridgeton, A county state of emergency was also declared. Over a dozen roadways were flooded and evacuations and water rescues occurred. Major roadways that were flooded and closed included State Routes 49 and 77. Many farm fields were submerged. Other hard hit municipalities included Greenwich, Stow Creek, Hopewell and Shiloh. Crops were also damaged, especially canning tomatoes. Damage was estimated at 20 million dollars. ||In Upper Deerfield Township, the torrential downpours started a domino effect of dam failures along the Cohansey River.  Seeley Lake was breached along Finley Road. The road was destroyed as the lake completely emptied. Downstream, the surge of water caused Sunset Lake to breach at West Park Drive in Bridgeton. This lead to the evacuation of approximately 150 residents along the Cohansey River within the city. A shelter was opened on Buckston Road. An approximately 1250 foot breach occurred along the river that flooded the Raceway within the Bridgeton City Park. The Cohanzick Zoo along the river was also flooded, but no animals were injured and the zoo itself was not seriously damaged. Flooding along Sunset Lake also led to the washout of a 75 foot by 100 foot section of Beebe Run Road within the city.  Event precipitation totals included 10.82 inches in Upper Deerfield and 10.63 inches in Seabrook.

More thunderstorms with heavy rain and extremely wet antecedent conditions caused additional flooding overnight on the 15th along the Raccoon Creek. County rainfall amounts averaged around one inch. The Raccoon Creek at Swedesboro was above its 13 foot flood stage from 140 a.m. EDT through 648 a.m. EDT on the 16th. It crested at 13.35 feet at 245 a.m. EDT.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms caused small stream and poor drainage flash flooding in lower Montgomery County. Several roads were closed and water rescues performed.  Fourteen county roads were closed due to flooding and there were fifty-three county dispatches for water rescues in Whitemarsh, Upper Dublin, Springfield, Abington and Upper Moreland Townships. In Plymouth Township, the ground floor of the Macy's was flooded at the Plymouth Meeting Mall.  The home furnishing, junior's and children's departments were damaged. The store closed early that evening, but reopened the next day.  No serious injuries were reported. In addition, The Wissahickon Creek at Fort Washington was briefly above its 9 foot flood stage from 1030 p.m. EDT through 1103 p.m. EDT on the 19th. It crested at 9.07 feet at 1045 p.m. EDT.  Event precipitation totals included 2.50 inches in Plymouth Meeting and 1.03 inches in Willow Grove.

Runoff from the heavy rain that fell in Montgomery County caused flooding along sections of the Wissahickon and Pennypack Creeks within Philadelphia. While event precipitation totals were less than one inch in Philadelphia, they reached between two and three inches in lower Montgomery County.  The Wissahickon Creek at its mouth was above its 5 foot flood stage from 857 p.m. EDT on the 19th through 328 a.m. EDT on the 20th. It crested at 5.28 feet at Midnight EDT on the 20th. The Pennypack Creek at the Rhawn Street Bridge was above its 7 foot flood stage from 1112 p.m. EDT on the 19th through 226 a.m. EDT on the 20th. It crested at 7.92 feet at 100 a.m. EDT on the 20th.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain across the northern half of Philadelphia caused poor drainage flooding and stream flash flooding along the Wissahickon, Frankford and Pennypack Creeks.  Event precipitation totals averaged 2 to 3.5 inches. The Frankford Creek at Castor Avenue had major flooding and was above its 7 foot flood stage from 316 p.m. EDT through 612 p.m. EDT on the 21st. It crested at 10.04 feet at 345 p.m. EDT.  The Wissahickon Creek at its mouth was above its 5 foot flood stage from 344 p.m. EDT through 1149 p.m. EDT on the 21st. It crested at 5.40 feet at 1000 p.m. EDT.  The Pennypack Creek at the Rhawn Street Bridge was above its 7 foot flood stage from 351 p.m. EDT through 404 p.m. EDT on the 21st. It crested at 7.12 feet at 400 p.m. EDT.  Event precipitation totals included 3.33 inches in Wyndmoor, 2.78 inches in Rockledge and 2.73 inches in Northeast Philadelphia.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain across the extreme lower part of Bucks County  caused poor drainage and small stream flash flooding. Event precipitation totals averaged 2 to 3 inches. Flooding was reported in Bensalem and Bristol.  In Bristol, the Mill Street parking lot as well as Farragut Avenue flooded. Several underpasses were also closed. Event precipitation totals included 2.51 inches in Bensalem and 2.46 inches in Penndel.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused field, poor drainage and small stream flash flooding in southwestern Kent County. A few roadways were flooded and closed. Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached 3 to 5 inches.

The Millstone River at Griggstown was above its 10 foot flood stage from 402 a.m. EDT on the 22nd through 712 p.m. EDT on the 23rd. It crested at 11.83 feet at 715 p.m. EDT on the 22nd.  Event precipitation totals included 2.91 inches in Princeton Township (Mercer County) and 1.48 inches in Montgomery Township.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused small stream flash flooding as well as poor drainage flooding in the southern half of Monmouth County. Howell, Ocean and Wall Townships were hardest hit with around a dozen homes damaged. The runoff also caused moderate flooding along the Manasquan River that lasted into the 22nd.||In Howell Township, the Mariner's Cove development near the Manasquan River was hard hit by flooding. Rescue boats were used to evacuate families as mud and water entered the first floor of homes. The U.S. Route 9 bridge over the Manasquan river was closed due to concern about its integrity. It was re-opened on the 22nd. Another bridge over the Manasuqan River on Allentown-Lakewood Road near Robert Brice Memorial Park was also flooded and closed.  In Ocean Township, flooding displaced residents of the Middlebrook at Monmouth Apartments on Deal Road. In Freehold, Post Road flooded by a creek and New Jersey State Route 33 was closed in both directions at Hills Mills Road. In Long Branch, 2nd Avenue was under three feet of water, the barricades were even floating away.   In Deal, New Jersey State Route 71 was closed in both directions. Streams were reported out of their banks in Millstone Township. ||Event precipitation totals included 4.61 inches in Howell Township, 3.75 inches in Ocean Township, 3.16 inches in Asbury Park and 2.96 inches in Eatontown.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused small stream flash flooding as well as poor drainage flooding in the northwest part of Ocean County. The runoff also caused flooding along the North Branch of the Metedeconk River that lasted into the 23rd.  In Jackson Township, vehicles became trapped in flood waters on six roadways: Bennetts Mills Road, Cedar Swamp Road, Chandler Road, County Line Road, Fox Hollow Drive and Nottingham Way.  The most concentrated flooding occurred in the Four Seasons Development. Six Flags, Great Adventure even closed early. No serious injuries were reported. Event precipitation totals included 3.85 inches in Jackson Township and 2.58 inches in Point Pleasant Beach.

The runoff from the heavy rain on the 21st caused flooding along the North Branch of the Metedeconk River.  Flooding occurred as far upstream as Aldrich Road (which was closed) in Jackson Township.  The North Branch of the Metedeconk River at  Lakewood was above its 7 foot flood stage from 622 p.m. EDT on the 22nd through 900 a.m. EDT on the 23rd. It crested at 7.42 feet at 10 p.m. EDT on the 22nd.

The runoff from the heavy rain on the 21st caused moderate flooding along the Manasquan River on the 22nd. The Manasquan River at Squankum had moderate flooding and was above its 7.5 foot flood stage from 117 a.m. EDT through 536 p.m. EDT on the 22nd. It crested at 9.94 feet at 1030 a.m. EDT.
A severe thunderstorm sheared off two poles on Cheney Road in Mannington Township.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down a couple of trees in western Pittsgrove Township around Centerton and Porchtown Roads. The combination of damaging winds and lightning caused about 1,200 customers to lose power in Salem County.

Lightning struck the television antenna of a home on Ayers Avenue in North Plainfield. The lightning traveled down the side of the home and entered into it through the metal dryer vent and set the lint on fire and burnt a hose. It also tripped the home's circuit breakers. Smoke filled the basement, but the firefighters' quick response confined the fire to the dryer.

A lightning strike and ensuing fire caused basement damage to one home on West Beechtree Lane in Radnor Township as well as a Sports Utility Vehicle next door. The lightning strike damaged a tree which fell on top of the vehicle. It then started a basement fire at the neighboring house. Four fire companies confined the smoke damage to the basement and some of the interior walls. No injuries were reported.

A lightning strike and ensuing fire damaged a home on Leon Avenue in Norwood Borough. Lightning struck the roof and the fire started in the attic. Five fire companies battled the blaze and the fire was confined to the second floor of the house, but water damage extended into the first floor.  No injuries were reported.

A lightning strike and ensuing fire gutted a house on Norwinden Drive in Springfield Township. Firefighters arrived and found the house fire fully involved. It took about thirty minutes to extinguish the blaze.  No injuries were reported.

A lightning strike and ensuing fire badly damaged a Maxim Road home in Howell. The fire started toward the rear of the home's attic and third floor and spread to the second floor before it was declared under control at 9 a.m. EDT. No serious injuries were reported.
The roof of a Drake Knoll home in Lewes was struck by lightning and started a fire. Five fire companies battled the blaze that was mainly confined to the roof. No serious injuries were reported.

Lightning struck the roof of a home on Bethlehem Pike in Fort Washington and started a fire. It took fire fighters about 30 minutes to extinguish the blaze. It was confined to the roof, although some holes had to be cut in the roof and walls to extinguish it. No serious injuries were reported.
Lightning struck a home in Newark and caused minor damage to it.

A lightning strike caused a fire at the Swiftwater Elementary Center in Paradise Township.  The fire was contained to the roof above the third grade classrooms. It was unsure if the damage was extensive enough to delay the start of school on August 29th.

A lightning strike started an insulation fire at a home on East Garfield Avenue in Atlantic Highlands.  Lightning struck a cable wire and traveled along it and ignited the home's insulation. Some smoke filled the home before the fire was extinguished.  No injuries were reported.
Lightning struck the Monmouth County 911 radio tower in Freehold.
A lightning strike knocked down a tree and wires across U.S. Route 46 in Liberty Township east of the Pequest Hatchery. The roadway was closed until the tree and wires were removed.

A lightning strike and ensuing fire badly damaged a home on Stone Run Drive in Rising Sun.  It took about thirty firefighters thirty minutes to extinguish the blaze. No serious injuries were reported.

A lightning strike and ensuing fire badly damaged a mobile home in Birch Court in Bainbridge. Lightning initially struck the roof of the mobile home above the bedroom. It took about thirty firefighters from four companies about fifteen minutes to get the fire under control. No serious injuries were reported.

A lightning strike to one of its water towers on Union Lane caused Brielle Borough to declare an emergency on the 21st. The lightning strike damaged electrical panels and also short circuited the entrance gate and a computer on the premises. The emergency was lifted on the 23rd after repairs were made.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a few trees in Stanton (Mill Creek Hundred) north of Kirkwood Highway and east of Limestone Road.

A severe thunderstorm tore the entire roof off a home on North Harrison Street in Wilmington. About a dozen trees were knocked down throughout the city. Five or six telephone poles were knocked down on Lancaster Avenue and one tree fell onto the northbound lanes of Interstate 95.

A pair of lightning strikes helped trigger fires that damaged two homes in Georgetown. One fire occurred on Avalon Drive and the second on Donaway Road. Four fire companies responded to each blaze. No injuries were reported.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down four trees and two wires onto roadways in Madison Township. It caused power outages in the downtown area of the township as well as causing about a dozen traffic lights to stop functioning. A wind gust of 50 mph was measured in neighboring Chatham Township.

The runoff from the heavy rain caused flooding in northern Gloucester County including the Mantua Creek basin.  A 55-year-old woman drowned after she drove into the swollen creek. Her body was recovered on the 15th. In West Deptford, a 30 foot by 15 foot sink hole caused a basement masonry wall collapse on Ellwood Avenue. Near the Mantua Creek, the southern end of the Willow Woods Mobile Home Park on Crown Point Road (New Jersey State Route 44) was flooded and evacuated. The roadway remained closed into the 15th. Paradise Road in West Deptford was also closed. Event precipitation totals in the Mantua Creek drainage basin averaged 4 to 5 inches.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused roadway, poor drainage and field flooding in the southern half of Camden County. Several roadways were flooded and closed, the most notable the White Horse Pike (U.S. Route 30).  Event precipitation totals included 8.04 inches in Winslow Township and 5.41 inches in Berlin Township.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams and roadways in Mount Olive Township. Several water rescues occurred throughout the township with some vehicles damaged by the flood waters. No serious injuries were reported. Event precipitation totals included 3.12 inches in Rockaway Township and 2.34 inches in Mount Olive Township.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours on already saturated grounds because of the remnants of Tropical Storm Lee produced small stream and poor drainage flooding in western Berks County mainly in Penn, Bern, North and Lower Heidelberg Townships. Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached 2 to 3 inches, most of which fell within an hour.
Quarter size hail fell just north of Newark during a severe thunderstorm.
A house was struck by lightning in Fair Hill. No serious injuries were reported.
Nickel size hail fell in Hainesport.
Nickel size hail fell in Pemberton Township.
Nickel size hail fell in Wrightstown Borough.
Nickel size hail fell at Fort Dix.
A severe thunderstorm dropped half dollar size hail in Juliustown (Springfield Township).
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a few trees and poles in Springfield Township.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a couple of trees in Pemberton.
Penny size hail fell in Honey Brook.
A severe thunderstorm dropped quarter size hail in West Brandywine Township.
A severe thunderstorm dropped quarter size hail in West Caln Township.
A severe thunderstorm dropped half dollar size hail in Downingtown.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down a couple of trees in West Brandywine Township.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down large tree limbs and wires in Drexel Hill (Upper Darby Township).
A severe thunderstorm dropped quarter size hail in Vernon Township.

A 40-year-old male construction worker was killed and two others were injured after they were struck by lightning while working on the Revel Casino Project in Atlantic City off of Connecticut Avenue. They were pouring concrete on the 7th floor when the bucket lift they were using was struck by lightning.

events.cz_name: LITTLE EGG INLET TO GREAT EGG INLET NJ OUT 20NM
events.event_narrative: A thunderstorm produced a wind gust of 39 knots (45 mph) as it moved across Point Point near Atlantic City.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down trees and power lines in Schnecksville (North Whitehall Township).

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding along many small streams in north central Hunterdon County. Stream flooding was reported in Lebanon, Glen Gardner, Clinton and Tewksbury.  There were a couple of camper rescues and vehicles were flooded. The runoff from the heavy rain also caused flooding along the South Branch of the Raritan River. Event precipitation totals included 3.99 inches in High Bridge, 3.94 inches in Clinton, 3.93 inches in Lebanon, 3.88 inches in Califon, 3.23 inches in Holland and 3.13 inches in Franklin.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding along smaller streams in southwestern Morris County in Washington and Mount Olive Townships. About a half dozen people had to be rescued from vehicles along River Road (South Branch of the Raritan River) in Mount Olive Township. Event precipitation totals included 4.99 inches in Mount Olive Township.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding along smaller streams and roadways in eastern Warren County mainly in Allamuchy, Franklin, Hackettstown, Independence and Mansfield Townships. In Franklin Township, residents of the Pohatcong Creek Mobile Home Adult Community were rescued by boat after that creek flooded.  Schools were closed in Mansfield Township. Homes along State Route 57 were flooded. In Hackettstown, the Trout Brook flooded U.S. Route 46 and Stiger Street. A half dozen roads were closed in the town and at least three cars were damaged. Some basements were also flooded. Both the Pequest and Musconetcong Rivers flooded again. The flooding rains also damaged the apple, corn and sod crops. Event precipitation totals included 4.91 inches in Blairstown, 4.77 inches in Hackettstown, 4.47 inches in Allamuchy and 4.21 inches in Mansfield.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding along smaller streams and roadways mainly in the eastern part of Sussex County. The heavy rain affected Andover, Byram, Green, Sparta and Stanhope the most. Several roads were also closed in Sparta and one school was evacuated because a nearby creek flooded. Ponds also overflowed in the township along Stanhope Road. In Andover Township, one home was evacuated along Limecrest Road.   Road closures were also reported in and around Newton because of the flooding. The runoff from the heavy rain also led to flooding along the Flat Brook that lasted into the 30th. Event precipitation totals included 4.16 inches in Andover and 3.83 inches in Newton.

Runoff from the heavier rain that fell earlier in the day on the 28th caused minor flooding along the South Branch of the Raritan River in Hunterdon County.  The South Branch of the Raritan River at High Bridge was above its 10 foot flood stage from 734 a.m. EDT through 815 p.m. EDT on the 28th. It crested at 11.18 feet at 3 p.m. EDT.  Farther downstream, the South Branch of the Raritan River at Stanton was above its 8 foot flood stage from 632 a.m. EDT on the 28th through 200 a.m. EDT on the 29th. It crested at 9.69 feet at 945 a.m. EDT on the 28th.

Runoff from the heavier rain that fell earlier in the day on the 28th in Hunterdon and Morris Counties caused minor flooding around the confluence of the North and South Branches of the Raritan River later in the day on the 28th. The North Branch of the Raritan River at the village of South Branch was above its 7 foot flood stage from 135 p.m. EDT through 830 p.m. EDT on the 28th. It crested at 7.46 feet at 630 p.m. EDT.

Runoff from the heavier rain that fell earlier in the day on the 28th caused minor flooding along the Flat Brook that lasted into the 30th. The Flat Brook at Flatbrookville was above its 6 foot flood stage from 640 p.m EDT on the 28th through 1204 p.m. EDT on the 30th. It crested at 6.54 feet at 1115 p.m. EDT on the 28th.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding from Bath through Bethlehem in the Monocacy Creek drainage basin. In Bath, water rescues and voluntary evacuations occurred. The Monocacy Creek flooded businesses and a senior high rise building. Flooding was also reported into the first floor of a few homes. Flooding was reported on Main, Chestnut and Northampton Streets. Downstream in East Allen Township, basement flooding up to twelve feet was reported.  In Bethlehem, the Monocacy Creek at Illicks Mill Road was above its 4.5 foot flood stage from 820 p.m. EDT through 950 p.m. EDT on the 28th. It crested at 4.94 feet at 915 p.m. EDT.  Event precipitation totals included 3.24 inches at the Lehigh Valley International Airport, 2.56 inches in Martins Creek and 1.74 inches in Bethlehem.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused poor drainage and small creek flash flooding in south central Monroe County, mainly in Ross and Chestnuthill Townships. Adjusted Doppler Radar storm total estimates averaged 3 to 4 inches in the townships. Event precipitation totals included 3.84 inches in Hamilton Township and 2.71 inches in Blakeslee.

Runoff from heavy rain that fell on the 28th caused major flooding along the Monocacy Creek in Bethlehem. It was the highest crest for the creek since the remnants of Hurricane Ivan in September of 2004. Once again the Industrial Colonial Quarter in Bethlehem was flooded. The Monocacy Creek in Bethlehem at Illicks Mill Road was above its 4.5 foot flood stage from 147 a.m. EDT through 6 p.m. EDT on the 29th. It crested at 7.66 feet at 515 a.m. EDT.

For the third time this month, runoff from heavy rain that fell on the 28th caused minor flooding in the headwaters of the Perkiomen Creek around the Green Lane Reservoir. The Main Stem of the Perkiomen Creek at East Greenville was above its 4.0 foot flood stage from 903 p.m. EDT on the 28th through 150 a.m. EDT on the 29th. It crested at 5.0 feet at 1145 p.m. EDT on the 28th.  The West Branch of the Perkiomen Creek at Hillegass was above its 5.0 foot flood stage from 631 p.m. EDT through 1006 p.m. EDT on the 28th. It crested at 5.31 feet at 830 p.m. EDT on the 28th.  Event precipitation totals included 3.53 inches in Pottstown, 2.43 inches in Gilbertsville and 1.71 inches in Green Lane.

The Christina River at Coochs Bridge had moderate flooding. The river was above its 10.5 foot flood stage from 844 p.m. EDT on the 23rd through 212 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 11.61 feet at 1130 p.m. EDT on the 23rd. Event precipitation totals included 3.56 inches in Clayton, 2.21 inches in Middletown and 1.65 inches at the New Castle County Airport.

Heavy rain caused flooding along the Pennypack Creek. The Pennypack Creek at the Rhawn Street Bridge was above its 7 foot flood stage from 945 p.m. EDT on the 23rd through 2 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 8.45 feet at 1230 a.m. EDT on the 24th. Event precipitation totals included 2.35 inches at the Philadelphia International Airport, 2.20 inches in Wyndmoor and 1.82 inches in Rockledge.

Heavy rain caused moderate flooding along the Manatawny Creek. The Manatawny Creek near Spangsville was above its 6 foot flood stage from 843 p.m. EDT on the 23rd through 504 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 7.31 feet at 1 a.m. EDT on the 24th. Event precipitation totals included 3.80 inches in Birdsboro, 2.98 inches in Oley and 2.04 inches in Fleetwood.

The runoff from the heavy rain on the 23rd caused minor flooding along sections of the Schuylkill River. The Schuylkill River at Norristown was above its 13 foot flood stage from 412 a.m. EDT through 1009 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 13.23 feet at 645 a.m. EDT. Event precipitation totals included 3.25 inches in Pottstown, 1.85 inches in Plymouth Meeting and 1.61 inches in Collegeville.

The runoff from the heavy rain on the 23rd caused minor flooding in the headwaters of the Perkiomen Creek around the Green Lane Reservoir. The Main Stem of the Perkiomen Creek at East Greenville was above its 4.0 foot flood stage from 902 p.m. EDT on the 23rd through 422 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 6.54 feet at Midnight EDT on the 24th. This was the 5th highest crest on record. The West Branch of the Perkiomen Creek at Hillegass was above its 5.0 foot flood stage from 908 p.m. EDT on the 23rd through 312 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 5.24 feet at 10 p.m. EDT on the 23rd. Event precipitation totals included 3.25 inches in Pottstown, 2.40 inches in Palm and 2.38 inches in Gilbertsville.

The runoff from the heavy rain on the 23rd caused numerous creeks in Chester County to flood with minor to moderate flooding occurring. The West Branch of the Brandywine Creek at Honey Brook had moderate flooding and was above its 7 foot flood stage from 707 p.m. EDT  on the 23rd through 310 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 10.65 feet at 930 p.m. EDT on the 23rd. Farther downstream, the West Branch of the Brandywine Creek at Coatesville was above its 7 foot flood stage from 757 p.m. EDT  on the 23rd through 5 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 7.82 feet at 2 a.m. EDT on the 24th. The East Branch of the Brandywine Creek below Downingtown had moderate flooding and was above its 7 foot flood stage from 1049 p.m. EDT  on the 23rd through 358 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 9.91 feet at 1115 a.m. EDT on the 24th. The main stem of the Brandywine Creek at Chadds Ford was above its 9 foot flood stage from 342 a.m. EDT through 516 p.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 10.91 feet at 1045 a.m. EDT.  The French Creek at Phoenixville was above its 8 foot flood stage from 1140 p.m. EDT on the 23rd through 926 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 9.62 feet at 3 a.m. EDT on the 24th. The Valley Creek at Valley Forge was above its 7 foot flood stage from 957 p.m. EDT  on the 23rd through 202 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 7.65 feet at 1115 p.m. EDT on the 23rd. Event precipitation totals included 4.39 inches in Nottingham, 2.97 inches in Unionville and 1.63 inches in West Chester.

The runoff from the heavy rain on the 23rd caused minor flooding on the Crum Creek and Main Stem of the Brandywine Creek on the 24th. The main stem of the Brandywine Creek at Chadds Ford was above its 9 foot flood stage from 342 a.m. EDT through 516 p.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 10.91 feet at 1045 a.m. EDT.  The Crum Creek near Newtown Square was above its 6 foot flood stage from 104 a.m. EDT through 202 a.m. EDT on the 24th. It crested at 6.23 feet at 129 a.m. EDT.   Event precipitation totals included 2.35 inches at the Philadelphia International Airport and 1.63 inches in Drexel Hill.

All of Port Deposit was evacuated because of the Susquehanna River flooding. Flood damage was reported in Port Deposit and Perryville. The Susquehanna River at the Conowingo Dam had major flooding, its third highest crest on record and its highest crest since January of 1996. The river was above its 23.5 foot flood stage from 438 p.m. EDT on the 7th through 130 a.m. EDT on the 12th. It crested at 32.41 feet at 515 a.m. EDT on the 9th.

The Christina River at Coochs Bridge had moderate flooding and was above its 10.5 foot flood stage from 527 p.m. EDT on the 6th through 743 a.m. EDT on the 7th. It crested at 11.8 feet at 945 p.m. EDT on the 6th. The Red Clay Creek at Stanton, just touched its 15 foot flood stage at Midnight EDT on the 7th. The entire event precipitation totals in New Castle County included 4.24 inches in Hockessin, 4.17 inches in Newark, 4.16 inches in Greenville, 3.48 inches in New Castle, 3.23 inches in Glasgow and 3.00 inches at the New Castle County Airport.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused flash flooding of roadways and fields in and mainly to the west of Seaford in western Sussex County. Sections of Stein Highway (Delaware State Route 20) and Figgs Road were among about a dozen roads that were closed by flash flooding. Many roadways within Seaford itself had high water on them. Delaware State Route 20 and Ellis Mill Road suffered washouts. The Seaford School District was closed the following day, September 9th. Doppler Radar storm total estimates for the entire event in the flash flood area exceeded 10 inches. Other event precipitation totals in Sussex County included 4.60 inches in Milford and 2.76 inches in Georgetown.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused poor drainage flooding and flash flooding of smaller streams in lower Lehigh County mainly in Lower Milford and Upper Saucon Townships. Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached 2 to 3 inches in this area.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused poor drainage flooding and flash flooding of smaller streams in lower Northampton County mainly in Williams and Lower Saucon Townships. Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached 2 to 3 inches in this area and event precipitation totals through the morning of the 6th included 2.87 inches in Glendon and 2.60 inches in Martins Creek.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused poor drainage flooding and flash flooding of smaller streams in extreme northern Montgomery County in Upper Hanover Township. The Perkiomen Creek at East Greenville was above its 4 foot flood stage from 916 p.m. EDT on the 5th through 344 a.m. EDT on the 6th. It crested at 5.57 feet at 1 a.m. EDT on the 6th. Event precipitation totals through the morning of the 6th included 3.00 inches in Palm.

Thunderstorms with very heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams as well as poor drainage flooding across eastern Sussex County from Green Township northeast through parts of Andover, Sparta, Hardyston and Vernon Townships. Event precipitation totals into the morning of the 6th included 3.25 inches in Vernon Township, 2.87 inches in Hopatcong, 2.80 inches in Hardyston Township and 2.70 inches in Andover Township.

Thunderstorms with very heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams as well as poor drainage flooding across Warren County from Harmony Township northeast through parts of White, Hope and Blairstown Townships. Event precipitation totals into the morning of the 6th included 3.31 inches in Knowlton Township, 2.98 inches in Blairstown Township, 2.95 inches in White Township and 2.92 inches in Liberty Township.

Repeating showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams and poor drainage areas in western Berks County during the afternoon and evening of the 7th. Twenty-four hour rainfall totals ending at 8 a.m. EDT on the 8th reached around 6 inches. Hardest hit were Bethel, Tulpehocken and Marion Townships. In Marion Township, water rescues were performed. Off of Canal Road within the township, a herd of cattle became stranded in a field. U.S. Route 422 was closed in Wolmelsdorf Borough.

Another band of showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams and poor drainage areas in the eastern half of Berks County during the late afternoon and evening of the 7th. Water rescues were performed in Cumru, Exeter (U.S. Route 422) and Oley Townships. Road closures occurred in Exeter, Ontelaunee, Cumru, Richmond and Greenwich Townships. In Reading, flash flooding was reported along Pennsylvania State Route 12. In Birdsboro, West Main Street was closed after the Hay Creek started to flood. Flooding along the Manatawny Creek was reported in Oley Township. The sewage system in Kutztown was getting overwhelmed.

A band of showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams and poor drainage areas in the western part of Chester County during the afternoon and early evening of the 7th. This initiated the flooding in the Brandywine Creek Basin.

A second band of showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams and poor drainage areas in the eastern part of Chester County during the late afternoon and early evening of the 7th. This also helped initiate and exacerbate the flooding in the Brandywine Creek Basin as well as along the Schuylkill River.

A band of showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams and poor drainage areas in the southern part of Montgomery County. Flooding occurred along the Wissahickon Creek and continued along the Schuylkill River. In Whitpain Township, along the Wissahickon Creek, 40 residents were evacuated on West Maple Street. Two buildings collapsed in Ambler Borough.

A band of showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams as well as poor drainage flooding in Philadelphia. It also caused the drowning death of a 27-year-old woman who was caught in flood waters in the East Germantown section of the city.  She was discovered in the rear of her Sports Utility Vehicle at the intersection of Musgrave and Haines Streets on the morning of the 8th.  The Wingohocking Creek, which is a creek that was buried underground during the 19th century had its waters back out of sewer grates and manhole covers in that section of the city.  Godfrey Avenue and Wister Street also flooded in East Germantown. The wall of a church also collapsed. Most gaged creeks within Philadelphia flooded as well as the Schuylkill River.

A band of showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams as well as poor drainage flooding in lower Bucks County. Flooding occurred in the Neshaminy Basin and the heavy rain helped exacerbate the ongoing or starting of flooding along the Delaware River. Along the Neshaminy Creek, in Langhorne, creek flooding reached the Bridgetown Mill House.

A band of showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams as well as poor drainage flooding in central Hunterdon County. Flooding started along the South Branch of the Raritan River and long term flooding along the Delaware River also started during the early morning of the 8th.

A band of showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding of smaller streams as well as poor drainage flooding in central Mercer County. Flooding started along the Assunpink Creek and long term flooding along the Delaware River also started during the early morning of the 8th.

The North Branch of the Rancocas Creek at Pemberton had a record breaking major flooding crest of 4.91 feet at 815 a.m. EDT on August 29th. The creek was above its 2.5 foot flood stage from 1145 p.m. EDT on August 27th through 645 p.m. EDT on September 1st.

For the second time within a month, the Maurice River at Norma had major flooding and set the second highest crest on record. The river at the Norma gage was above its 4 foot flood stage from 1115 p.m. EDT on August 27th through 1030 a.m. EDT on September 2nd.  It crested at 7.72 feet at 400 p.m. EDT on August 29th.

For the second time within a month, the Maurice River at Norma had major flooding and set the second highest crest on record. The river at the Norma gage was above its 4 foot flood stage from 1115 p.m. EDT on August 27th through 1030 a.m. EDT on September 2nd.  It crested at 7.72 feet at 400 p.m. EDT on August 29th.

For the second time within a month, the Great Egg Harbor River at Folsom had record breaking major flooding. It was above its 6 foot flood stage from 1005 a.m. EDT on August 28th through 415 a.m. EDT on September 1st. It crested at 8.27 feet at 1115 p.m. EDT on August 29th.

The Pompton River had major flooding and record breaking crests throughout its entire length, surpassing the flooding that occurred during April of 1984. The river at Pompton Plains receded below flood stage before the start of September.  The Pompton River at Ryerson Road crested at a record breaking 20.47 feet at 1140 p.m. EDT on August 28th. It was above its 12 foot flood stage from 713 a.m. EDT on August 28th through 602 a.m. EDT on September 3rd. It was above its 8 foot flood stage from 908 a.m. EDT on August 28th through 739 a.m. EDT on September 4th. The Passaic River at Millington and Pine Brook had major flooding and record breaking crests. The Passaic River at Chatham had moderate flooding. The Passaic River at Millington record breaking crest of 10.26 feet occurred at 1 p.m. EDT on August 29th. It was above its 8 foot flood stage from 708 a.m. EDT on August 28th through 407 a.m. EDT on September 1st. The Passaic River at Chatham was above its 6 foot flood stage from 232 a.m. EDT on August 28th through 930 a.m. EDT on September 3rd. It crested at 7.76 feet at 1245 p.m. EDT on August 29th. It was above its 19 foot flood stage from 730 a.m. EDT on August 28th through 1115 p.m. EDT on September 5th, just before the rains from Tropical Storm Lee arrived. The Passaic River was the last river and Pine Brook was the last location on the river to go below flood stage. Just downstream of Morris County along the Passaic and Union County line, the Passaic River at Two Bridges also had major flooding and a record breaking crest of 17.17 feet at 515 a.m. EDT on August 30th. It was above its 9 foot flood stage from 7 a.m. EDT on August 28th through 815 a.m. EDT on September 5th.

A severe thunderstorm damaged three building roofs at the Devereux Mapleton School along Sugartown Road in Willistown Township.  Most of the damage was to a maintenance building where approximately 50 percent of the roof was blown off.  In addition, a localized power outage occurred in the area.  No injuries were reported.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down approximately a dozen large trees up to 70 feet tall along a park entrance on the Ambler and Upper Dublin Township border.
A severe thunderstorm knocked down several trees at The Woodlands in Horsham Township.

Lightning struck the Whitehall Township municipal building on the afternoon of the 28th. The thunderstorm produced several strikes that hit township buildings on MacArthur Road and a propane tank at the public works building which caused an underground tank fire. The municipal building was struck, but suffered no apparent damage. The building was evacuated as a precaution. Another lightning strike caused a loss of power to a fuel pump on the township building's property.  No injuries were reported.

An EF-0 tornado touched down in Queen Anne's County, northeast of Centreville around 830 p.m. EDT.  The tornado began just north of Shellcross Farm Lane and tracked about 5 miles northeast to between Route 19 and Route 302 before dissipating, remaining on the west side of Route 301.  Near the beginning of the tornado's path, in the 1200-block of White Marsh Road, the roof on one side of a large pole barn was torn off.  Its debris was scattered for a quarter to a half mile in all directions and damaged a nearby home.  Minor to moderate structural damage also occurred to several homes, barns, and outbuildings along Granny Branch Road, Route 405, and Route 19.  Damage to fencing and an overturned irrigation system was also observed along Route 405.  In addition, numerous trees were either snapped or uprooted along the tornado's 5-mile long path.  The tornado's maximum path width was about 50 yards, with a maximum estimated wind speed of 80 mph.  No injuries were reported.

The Griggstown Causeway was closed because of this flooding. Event precipitation totals included 2.87 inches in Hillsborough Township, 2.71 inches in Montgomery Township, 2.30 inches in Franklin Township, 2.20 inches in Bedminster Township, 2.06 inches in Somerville, 1.97 inches in Bridgewater Township and 1.56 inches in Bernards Township.

The runoff from thunderstorms with heavy rain between 630 p.m. EDT and 830 p.m. EDT on the 15th in Upper Bucks County caused minor flooding along the East Branch of the Perkiomen Creek later that evening.  The East Branch of the Perkiomen Creek near Dublin was above its 5 foot flood stage from 933 p.m. EDT through 950 p.m. EDT on the 15th. It crested at 5.09 feet at 945 p.m. EDT. Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached around 2 inches in a narrow band from Sellersville east through Pipersville.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding in extreme southeast Chester County overnight on the 15th with Tredyffrin and Easttown Townships hit the hardest. There were eight water rescues as flash flooding occurred along the headwaters of the Valley and Darby Creeks.  The Valley Creek at Valley Forge was above its 7 foot flood stage from 1252 a.m. EDT through 207 a.m. EDT on the 16th. It crested at 7.91 feet at 130 a.m. EDT.  Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached around 3.5 inches in those townships.

In the township, flash flooding was reported along South Gulph Road as Gulph Creek flooded  Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached around 3.5 inches in the township. Actual event totals included 3.46 inches in Norristown and 2.07 inches in West Norriton.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding along the Frankford Creek in Philadelphia. Urban and poor drainage flooding occurred elsewhere in the city.  The Frankford Creek at Castor Avenue was above its 7 foot flood stage from 225 a.m. EDT through 255 a.m. EDT on the 16th. It crested at 7.9 feet at 245 a.m. EDT.   Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached around 2.5 inches in the northern part of the city. Actual event totals included 2.57 inches in Rockledge, 2.43 inches in Rhawnhurst and 2.26 inches at the Northeast Philadelphia Airport.

Thunderstorms with heavy downpours caused flash flooding in extreme northern Delaware County and included the headwaters of the Darby Creek as well as Crum Creek. Hardest hit were Radnor and Newtown Townships.  Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached around 3.5 inches in the northern part of those townships.  The Crum Creek near Newtown Square was above its 5 foot flood stage from 141 a.m. EDT through 543 a.m.. EDT on the 16th. It crested at 7.57 feet at 245 a.m. EDT.

Minor flooding along the Crum Creek continued into the early morning hours of the 16th. The Crum Creek near Newtown Square was above its 5 foot flood stage from 141 a.m. EDT through 543 a.m.. EDT on the 16th. It crested at 7.57 feet at 245 a.m. EDT.

A lightning strike caused a three-alarm fire at the Dow Chemical facility on Pennsylvania State Route 413 and State Road in the Croydon section of Bristol Township. A lightning bolt struck two of the storage tanks at the plant. The ensuing fire badly damaged two large 250,000 gallon tanks that held chemicals used in the manufacturing of acrylic paint products. The fire damaged gaskets, lines and protective ground liners outside the tanks and allowed flammable chemicals to leak into the nearby air, ground and on-site surface water. The fire consumed a significant amount of the more than one million pounds of ethyl acrylate and butyl acrylate in the storage tanks.  A 65-year-old fire police captain with the Bristol Fire Company, left the scene after feeling ill and later that day died of a fatal heart attack. Firefighters and hazmat teams from three counties responded to the blaze and worked with Dow���s in-house emergency response fire and hazmat teams to quell the flames and contain the two chemicals that were in the tanks. Three emergency workers suffered minor injuries. The blaze was declared under control shortly after 7 a.m. EDT that morning. Early in the day, the Bucks County Emergency Management and the Bucks County Health Department advised residents who live near the site of the fire to remain indoors due to the potential for the two chemicals to cause minor throat or eye irritation, headaches and nausea. The chemical odor from the fire, which was smelled in both Pennsylvania and across the river in New Jersey in Mercer, Burlington and Monmouth Counties.  The smell dissipated as the day continue.  Due to the chemical odor, all schools in Bristol Borough were closed on the 16th.

The heaviest rain fell in Upper Hanover Township and also in East Greensville, Pennsburg and Red Hill Boroughs.  The main stem of the Perkiomen Creek at East Greenville was above its 4 foot flood stage from 533 a.m. EDT through 725 a.m. EDT on the 27th. It crested at 4.17 feet at 6 a.m. EDT.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused poor drainage as well as small creek flash flooding in and around East Stroudsburg. Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached around 4.5 inches.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours hit Hamilton Township the hardest in Monroe County as Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached between 6 and 7 inches during the afternoon of the 26th.  Multiple roadways were flooded and included Pennsylvania State Route 33 between Syndersville and Interstate 80. The roadway was closed for nearly two hours and reopened at 620 p.m. EDT that evening. Beaver Valley Road between Turkey Hill Road and Haney Road was closed because it was undermined by a flooding creek. The combination of damaging winds, flooding rains and lightning caused about 2.000 Pennsylvania Power and Light and Metropolitan Edison customers to lose power.  The Pocono Creek near Brislin Road in Stroud Township crested at 10.99 feet. There is no established flood stage for the creek at that site. An event total of 3.23 inches was measured in Syndersville in Hamilton Township.
Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused flash flooding of smaller streams in Pocono Township. Doppler Radar storm total estimates reached two inches within 45 minutes within the township.

Thunderstorms with torrential downpours caused flash flooding of smaller streams as well as extensive poor drainage flooding in Lansford and Summit Hill Boroughs and the northwest part of Mahoning Township. Roadways were closed and many basements were flooded. In Summit Hill, Pennsylvania State Route 902 was shut down for two and a half hours because of debris and rocks pushed onto the roadway. A portion of Oak Street was also closed. Firefighters responded to thirty-six calls of flooded basements. The annual Stay At Home Festival never opened because volunteers had to rebuild the stands and the field was swamped by flood waters. In Lansford, there was four feet of water on U.S. Route 209 and one motorist had to be rescued.  Other roadways in the borough were damaged by flooding as asphalt was washed away. A storm total measurement of 7.40 inches was measured in Lansford.

A severe thunderstorm knocked down a few trees and wires in Jackson Township, the hardest hit township in Monroe County by the thunderstorms that evening. One downed tree took down power lines on Mountain Springs Drive and Cardinal Lane. About 50 customers in the township lost power.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding in the headwaters of the Perkiomen Creek in northern Montgomery County. The Perkiomen Creek at East Greenville started flooding at 107 a.m. EDT on the 2nd and the West Branch of the Perkiomen Creek at Hillegass started flooding at 135 a.m. EDT on the 2nd.

Runoff flooding from the heavy rain that fell overnight on the 1st persisted into the morning of the 2nd in the headwaters region of the Perkiomen Creek.  The Main Stem of the Perkiomen Creek at East Greenville was above its 4 foot flood stage from 107 a.m. EDT through 806 a.m. EDT on the 2nd. It crested at 6.13 feet at 5 a.m. EDT on the 2nd.   The West Branch of the Perkiomen Creek at Hillegass was above its 5 foot flood stage from 135 a.m. EDT through 250 a.m. EDT on the 2nd and again from 6 a.m. EDT through 720 a.m. EDT on the 2nd. Its respective crests were 5.16 feet at 2 a.m. EDT and 5.08 feet at 630 a.m. EDT. Farther downstream, the East Branch of the Perkiomen Creek at Schwenksville crested just below its 7 foot flood stage (6.97 feet) at 8 a.m. EDT on the 2nd. Event precipitation totals included 2.30 and 2.09 inches in Gilbertsville.

Showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain caused flash flooding and roadway flooding near and along smaller creeks in Alburtis, Macungie, Lower and Upper Macungie Townships. Event precipitation totals included 2.78 inches in Orefield and 2.02 inches at the Lehigh Valley International Airport.
Heavy rain caused poor drainage. roadway and field flooding in Pittsgrove Township. A Cocorahs observer measured 4.63 inches of rain within the township.

Heavy rain caused poor drainage. roadway and field flooding in Upper Deerfield Township. Water rescues occurred along New Jersey State Route 77. Event totals included 5.43 inches in Upper Deerfield and 2.71 inches at Seabrook Farms. The Cohansey River at Seeley crested at 7.11 feet at 515 a.m. EDT on the 13th. The estimated flood stage is 6 feet.

It crested at 12.00 feet at 130 a.m. EDT on the 13th. Event precipitation totals included 4.60 inches in Saint Georges Hundred,  4.06 inches in Glasglow, 3.31 inches in Newark and 1.48 inches at the New Castle County Airport.

Multiple thunderstorms produced torrential downpours and flash flooding in eastern parts of Stafford, Barnegat and Ocean Townships. Five inches of rain was reported within ninety minutes. Motorists were stranded within their vehicles with water rising to nearly window level in Manahawkin in Stafford Township. Multiple roadways were closed including New Jersey State Route 72 in Stafford Township.Ten vehicles were so badly flooded that they had to be towed away from the Ocean Acres section of Stafford Township. New Jersey State Route 72, Forecastle and Outboard Avenues remained closed into the evening of the 22nd.  This inhibited weekend getaway traffic to Long Beach Island as this occurred on a Friday.  No serious injuries were reported. Two CoCoRahs reports from Stafford Township had event totals of 7.60 inches and 5.77 inches respectively.

A thunderstorm with very heavy downpours caused flash flooding of roadways and small creeks in Upper Deerfield Township. A Skywarn spotter reported several roadways were flooded.

A strong thunderstorm knocked down one tree onto a house on Montrose Lane in the Millbrook Park section of Willingboro Township.  Doppler Radar suggested the wind gusts were around 45 mph. No injuries were reported.

A gust front outrunning a cluster of severe thunderstorms entered the Tilghman Island area of western Talbot County at approximately 11:22 pm EDT on the 29th.  This gust front produced damaging wind gusts estimated at 65 mph as it traversed eastward across the county.  Within approximately 20 minutes of the gust front passage, a potent line of severe thunderstorms tracked eastward through Talbot County, producing another round of destructive wind gusts, estimated at 65 mph.  A significant number of trees and electric wires were reported down county-wide with damage first being noted on Tilghman Island.  Severe thunderstorms exited eastern Talbot County, including the town of Matthews, at approximately 12:31 am EDT on the 30th.

A gust front outrunning a cluster of severe thunderstorms entered near Stevensville in western Queen Anne's County at approximately 11:22 pm EDT on the 29th. This gust front produced damaging wind gusts estimated at 65 mph as it traversed eastward across the county. Within approximately 20 minutes of the gust front passage, a potent line of severe thunderstorms tracked eastward through Queen Anne's County, producing another round of destructive wind gusts, estimated at 65 mph. Large tree limbs and electric wires were reported down across the county, with damage initially reported in the Stevensville area. Damage to a large chimney and the exterior walls of a home was also reported in Stevensville. Severe thunderstorms exited eastern Queen Anne's County, including the town of Sudlersville, at approximately 12:31 am EDT on the 30th.

A gust front outrunning a cluster of severe thunderstorms entered near Rock Hall in western Kent County at approximately 11:22 pm EDT on the 29th. This gust front produced damaging wind gusts estimated at 65 mph as it traversed eastward across the county. Within approximately 20 minutes of the gust front passage, a potent line of severe thunderstorms tracked eastward through Kent County, producing another round of destructive wind gusts, estimated at 65 mph. Many large tree limbs were reported down across the county, including in the Millington area. Severe thunderstorms exited eastern Kent County, near Massey, at approximately 12:31 am EDT on the 30th. A peak wind gust of 66 mph was measured at Tolchester Beach.

A gust front outrunning a cluster of severe thunderstorms entered near Harmony in western Caroline County at approximately 11:40 pm EDT on the 29th. This gust front produced damaging wind gusts estimated at 65 mph as it traversed eastward across the county. Within approximately 20 minutes of the gust front passage, a potent line of severe thunderstorms tracked eastward through Caroline County, producing another round of destructive wind gusts, estimated at 65 mph. Trees and electric wires were reported down across the county. Severe thunderstorms exited eastern Caroline County, including the town of Henderson, at approximately 12:49 am EDT on the 30th.

A gust front outrunning a cluster of severe thunderstorms entered near Port Deposit in western Cecil County at approximately 11:27 pm EDT on the 29th. This gust front produced damaging wind gusts estimated from 65 to 70 mph as it traversed eastward across the county. Within approximately 20 minutes of the gust front passage, a potent line of severe thunderstorms tracked eastward into Cecil County. One thunderstorm cell in particular experienced rapid intensification and expansion as it tracked from around Baltimore, MD across Cecil County and into northern Delaware. Destructive wind gusts, estimated at 70 mph, resulted in significant tree and power line damage county-wide. Approximately 35 roads were impassable due to numerous downed trees. In Chesapeake City, several large trees fell onto homes, resulting in one injury. A tree also fell onto a house in the town of North East. Damage to multiple buildings was reported in Warwick, and a large concentration of downed trees was reported in Cecilton. Severe thunderstorms exited eastern Cecil County, including the town of Elkton, at approximately 12:40 am EDT on the 30th.  A young man was critically injured on the morning of July 2 around 330 am EDT when a tree branch fell on his tent at Camp Rodney in Elk Neck State Park in Northeast, Maryland. It is believed that the tree was weakened by the derecho that went through the night of the 29th.

A gust front outrunning a cluster of severe thunderstorms entered near Newark in western New Castle County at approximately 11:57 pm EDT on the 29th. This gust front produced damaging wind gusts estimated from 65 to 70 mph as it traversed eastward across the county. Within approximately 20 minutes of the gust front passage, a potent line of severe thunderstorms tracked eastward into New Castle County. One thunderstorm cell in particular experienced rapid intensification and expansion as it tracked into New Castle County. Destructive wind gusts, estimated near 75 mph, resulted in tree and power line damage across the county. Multiple downed trees were reported in Middletown and Odessa. In addition, power poles were snapped by wind gusts estimated between 70 and 75 mph in Middletown. Severe thunderstorms exited eastern New Castle County, including Delaware City, at approximately 12:50 am EDT on the 30th.
